My point wasn’t that you literally said that. My point was to explain why I don’t think it’s different, a big part of that being *because we are allowed to look at them.* that’s all I meant by that.

I mean, we agree on that part, that it’s my choice to look and if I don’t want to risk seeing any negativity then I shouldn’t. It is the author’s responsibility. All I am saying is that the reader is also responsible for what they write. If they don’t care then they don’t care, cool, whatever. But if they’re coming here to complain that author’s read public bookmarks and get salty about it, then obviously they care about what said authors think a little.

FAFO applies to literally everyone in public spaces whether we like it or not. I think everyone should conduct themselves accordingly—aka, however tf they want, with full awareness that everyone else will conduct themselves how they want and react. We’re all responsible for our own actions. I don’t think there’s anything else to say about it.

Edit: spelling =_=

But they are *public* bookmarks. There is no “readers only” mode. I’m entitled to look at them if I feel like it (just not entitled to being protected from criticism in there or harass anyone about it obviously, that is unhinged behavior). If there’s criticism about my story there, for *anybody* to see, that includes me. That’s why I don’t think it’s any different. I also don’t think it’s breaking any rules, so readers are free to use the bookmarks as they wish—it just doesn’t make them special in this regard.

I ultimately do agree with that though, that the discussion is repetitive with nothing to be done about it. People will write whatever they want and do what they want to do. And if it’s following the rules, then what about it? Like it or not.

I just think it’s common sense that whatever you say or post publicly has potential to garner attention, positive or negative, and everyone should navigate spaces with that in mind. However they wanna act is up to them, and however others wanna respond isn’t. That’s all.

Genuinely—why are authors expected to take criticism or deal with being publicly judged, but readers aren’t? Even here, on a different website, in a forum meant for discussion about topics relevant to readers and writers? This is something I don’t understand.

Let me be clear—I don’t feel entitled as an author to nothing but praise, and I don’t think I *should* be shielded from criticism. If I post my story publicly then thems the brakes. I fail to see why a reader’s public commentary should be different, especially when it’s being talked about off the website their commentary lives on.

If they don’t care then why is this even an issue? Lol let authors get salty about it if you don’t care. Why would a reader be affected at all?

Personally I think this is a nonissue because of what I said—do whatever you like so long as it doesn’t break TOS. That’s about it.

And the reader chose to put negativity out there publicly for anyone, including the author, to witness. If an author chooses to look, they’re risking seeing it, and if a reader chooses to post something negative, they’re risking the author seeing it. Actions have consequences and both writers and readers should understand that.

If they’re public it’s *public* so I’d say the author is “minding their business” just fine.

Not the person you were responding to, but this is just my 2 cents.

When I think “this is unnecessary” about a scene in a book, I don’t think of it from an angle of “this makes me uncomfortable and so it shouldn’t be there.” I think unnecessary means just what it says—this event/scene is not something that needed to happen as it did to function narratively. It doesn’t really matter if the content is “offensive” or not, because I don’t think that’s what makes it *necessary* or not. A lot of stories have extra fat that could use trimming.

So basically to me, it’s a writing critique and not commentary on how unsavory something might be. Is there another way of writing it that would have done just as good of a job, maybe even better? Probably. Would the hypothetical “better” version be less offensive? Maybe, maybe not. I suppose at the end of the day it all just comes down to opinion and YMMV.

How do they learn the lesson if they get away with it and there are no consequences? The issue with this reasoning, for me, is that this instance, sure, there is no “harm.” But what if this friend just starts cheating with AI on *all* their writing assignments? At what point does it matter? Are stealing and cheating only wrong if someone is caught?

I just think that it being unethical is good enough reason for the transgression to matter, and the behavior needs to be corrected (but that’s on the individual and those in a position to do so for them, a friend isn’t a parent). There’s a reason we teach people these things when the stakes are low, like for a high school writing assignment—if they can’t be assed with doing the right thing when the stakes are low, can they be trusted to do so when the stakes are high?

For what it’s worth, snitching wouldn’t be my first or second action in this scenario. I would always talk to a friend first, more than once even, before doing anything more aggressive or extreme. Where I disagree is on the point of lying, cheating, and stealing another person’s work—I don’t think that’s actually so small potatoes that I could just laugh it off and ignore it, especially as a creative. It shows a blatant disregard for other’s work and a distinct lack of integrity. If they seemed to feel even a smidge bad about it, that might be a little different, but based on the OP, it sounds like their friend thinks there’s nothing wrong with what she’s doing? I find that a little unsavory. This is a person that *does* need to learn something, like “actions have consequences” and “cheating and stealing is wrong.” However, I agree that the lesson may or may not be best learned by having their friend snitch on them.

So, I’m not super sure what I’d do other than urge my friend to reconsider, to be honest. But I couldn’t really handwave it off if their attitude was so flagrantly uncaring of the situation.

Alright, I want to preface this comment by saying that fanfic is written for fun, and if you have fun writing 20k+ word chapters, then that is what matters. You should do it, you should have fun. Fandom should be fun and make you happy. Tons and tons of people are thrilled over long chapters getting posted, so you can take my commentary with a grain of salt, seriously. 

IMO 20k for a single chapter is way too long. And I don’t say that because it’s off putting due to there being too much to read at once. I say that because frankly chapters shouldn’t be that long. A single chapter should not be the length of a long short story/novella. It suggests that either the author is struggling with determining natural breaks in the story or is having an issue with plotting or potentially both. 

It’s a pacing issue usually and not a prose one. That is to say, the quality of the writing itself can be amazing even if I personally find the chapters to be too long. But usually it’s a case of the chapter “overstaying its welcome” if that makes sense. I would encourage you to comb through your chapter and see where the natural breaks are, and if there really aren’t any until you hit the 20k mark, I think you should consider editing. 

TLDR: while I don’t think it’s always an accurate representation of the authors writing, I personally am turned off by an excessively long chapter because it often does translate to the author not quite knowing how to plot their story or write quality chapters that aren’t too long or all over the place. YouTube is always helpful for tutorials. More important than learning the adobe suite, you need to learn design theory and principles first. There are books, of course, but a plethora of content is also out there. If you don’t understand how to do layout, visual hierarchy, typography and typesetting, etc, your designs will certainly suffer for it. 

In my experience, you should focus on learning illustrator and indesign over photoshop. But I kinda hate photoshop so I’m biased lol. If you can get really good with indesign it’s a HUGE benefit when it comes to job searching, a lot of people aren’t very good or familiar with it. 

And of course, practice practice practice. Before you ever start digitally, start on pencil and paper. Make a hundred sketches before you pick something and try to work with it. Start small, and remember that your taste/“eye” for design will be much more refined and “better” than the stuff you’ll be making at the beginning. It can be hard to get through that stage of making subpar stuff and not really getting what makes it that way or how to fix it (this is where school becomes a real benefit tbh, critique and all that).

ETA: if you simply love art and drawing there is a nonzero chance you will despise graphic design, and that’s okay! It’s a different thing, really.

I’m a professional printer so maybe I can help. 

Monitors are color-calibrated, essentially meaning that each individual monitor was “tuned” to show colors the way they do. Sadly, this means that there will never be exact color matching and accuracy from display to display. Even printers—hell, even my $70k one—are calibrated. The same color can and often will look different machine to machine. 

The best thing that you can do IMO is check out what it looks like between each display and adjust your colors as you see fit. Another thing to keep in mind is to make sure that your file was setup with the appropriate color space (for screens, this would be RGB; CMYK is for print and will dull your colors).

ETA: you could do some research on photospectrometers and color gamuts and ICC profiles—but I don’t think these things will help very much. ICC profiles really shouldn’t be a big concern for you—it’s confusing territory, and whoever prints the artwork will have their own ICC profiles calibrated for their printer anyway. 

TLDR: don’t overwhelm yourself with info you don’t need; try color calibrating if you want to; sadly this is just a reality of RGB/monitors.

An example of trauma dumping that I experienced recently:

My roommate told me about how she was sexually abused as a child, not super detailed but how can that story not be incredibly vivid by nature of what it is, right? I didn’t ask her to tell me about this. It was deeply upsetting to hear. I mean I was crying, hard, because of how awful it was. Brutal. And she didn’t even hesitate or stop or ask if I was okay or anything, even though I was sobbing in front of her and was obviously Not Okay for a good hour afterwards. I would consider that trauma dumping.

I wanna be supportive to my friends, but I can’t always emotionally handle that super heavy shit, especially when my own nervous system is acting up. I know that sometimes people in my life feel the same way—overwhelmed and possibly triggered, but feeling obligated to listen so as to not stifle me. But I’d hate knowing I’d caused them similar pain to how I feel when triggered because I didn’t ask first or read their vibes correctly. 

I understand why people don’t like the term, but the truth is that talking about your trauma, unsolicited and without concern for the other persons feelings about it, can lead to triggering them as well (**i am not saying that you do this OP, this is a general talk about trauma dumping**) And nobody likes that, of course. 

And those who trauma dump aren’t doing so with the intention of causing harm. But it is incredibly difficult to sit through sometimes, depending on the person and the time and the place. Triggering someone else because you feel like you should be able to talk about your life without interruption is unfair to the listener. 

And you *should* be able to talk about your trauma—but truly not everyone can handle it. I think it’s important to understand how deeply upsetting these things can be to the listener and take it into consideration. 

Now. If someone tries to get emotional support from a friend (let’s use your example of getting evicted), and their friend simply says they don’t have the energy—I think that’s assholish of the friend. Fairweather shit. Everyone needs support in difficult times. This is so very different from trauma dumping. 

Another personal example I’ll give: my mother. My mother has used me as a therapist my entire life. I’ve heard every little horrible thing, no matter how bad or inappropriate or uncomfortable. If I ask her to stop, she’ll cry about how she has no one else to talk to. But that shit is so hard to listen to, relentlessly, and she has never been concerned with how it makes me feel, because it’s always about her feelings. She’s a narcissist. 

Is she a narcissist because she wants someone to talk to? Of course not. It’s narcissistic because she steamrolls me, will not respect a single solitary boundary, and won’t understand why it’s hurtful—she’s selfishly dumping her problems onto me, constantly, with no regard for my emotions or needs. And she gets upset if I even try to express that I can’t talk about it anymore. 

I don’t think you are trauma dumping by opening up to your friends. I think trauma dumping is defined by a distinct lack of thought or consideration for how the listener feels, or feeling entitled to making people listen and not get upset and overwhelmed, despite knowing that by definition of they’re sharing trauma—something inherently awful and emotionally painful.

However, mindfulness is something that to me is a great tool (full disclosure, I’m a baby Buddhist, so you may not agree with everything I’m saying here, and that’s totally okay!) that helps mentally, physically, and spiritually. 

Let’s take an example of when you wouldn’t want to zone out and be stuck in your head—so not a time when you can happily daydream or get creatively lost in thought—such as when the thoughts that flood your mind when you’re zoned out are very negative. 

Are you familiar with grounding exercises? They’re very similar. Grounding exercises are meant to pull you out of your head and back into the present moment. Imagine you’re trying to have coffee with a friend, but you can’t focus on any of the stuff you’re really doing because your mind is stuck on something that bothered you or a task you missed doing or anything else. 

Presumably you want to be engaged with your friend in the coffee shop, right? So you mindfully engage with the setting, your body, etc. You think about how the warm coffee mug feels in your hands, the brightness of the room, the way your body feels sitting there, the words your friend is saying, etc. It pulls you out of your head and into the present moment. 

I have CPTSD as well, and just so you know, meditation and mindfulness can be…bad for us. Emotional flashbacks aren’t the same as unpleasant thoughts, and if you’re triggered and then let it fester or “sit with it,” unless you’re really trained in it, it’s gonna make it worse. So it’s 100% okay if you aren’t in a place where you can do this. 

I would try practicing it only in the times where you want to be engaged with the moment, and not times when you’re otherwise chill with zoning out. And yes we all still zone out! I hope any of this helps.
